The Congo Crisis erupted from 1960 to 1965 following the Democratic Republic of the Congo's sudden independence from Belgium. Political factions, provincial governments, and foreign powers competed for control. Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba's assassination, a secession movement in resource-rich Katanga Province, and superpower intervention transformed what might have been a regional conflict into a proxy battleground of the Cold War. The Congo gained independence from Belgium on June 30th, 1960, with minimal preparation or indigenous administrative infrastructure, creating an immediate power vacuum. Patrice Lumumba, the Congo's first Prime Minister and independence hero, represented radical nationalism and Pan-African ideals, alarming Western powers and Belgian business interests. The Katanga Province, led by Moises Tshombe and backed by Belgian mining corporations, seceded in July 1960, claiming independence. This secession became the crisis's center. Lumumba appealed to the Soviet Union for military aid after the United Nations refused decisive intervention, prompting Western and Western-aligned African nations to view him as a communist threat. Joseph Desire Mobutu, a military officer, orchestrated a coup in September 1960 and imprisoned Lumumba. Lumumba was murdered in January 1961 under circumstances implicating Belgian forces and CIA involvement. The United Nations deployed a peacekeeping force called ONUC but remained hamstrung by Security Council divisions and limited mandate. UN troops eventually fought Katangan secessionists. Superpower rivalry turned the Congo into a Cold War battleground, with the United States supporting Mobutu against Soviet-supported factions, and various African nations choosing sides based on Cold War alignment. Mobutu gradually consolidated power, establishing authoritarian rule from 1965 to 1997 that plagued the Congo with endemic corruption, economic mismanagement, and persistent regional instability. The crisis demonstrated how Cold War rivalries could complicate decolonization, as superpowers prioritized geopolitical competition over African autonomy and sovereignty.
